messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 70
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Welder
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Entrapment: Having no options, Violence: Violence, Auditory/Threat: Gunshot noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories, Fawn Response: become overly compliant when feeling threatened, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Forty years ago, Mateo had found himself pressed against a concrete wall in a windowless room, his wrists bound in coarse wire that dug deeper with every futile pull. There had been no exit, no gap to slip through, only the heavy silence and the sudden, sharp reports of firearms firing in the adjacent corridor. He remembered the dry heat of the space, the dust coating his tongue, and the way his mind had quietly lifted away from the blows, sliding into a thick, numb distance so he would not have to feel them. When the men finally left, he told himself it was his own fault, that if he had kept his posture lower, if he had chosen his words differently, none of it would have happened. He carried that certainty with him when he returned to the United States, settling in a quiet neighborhood where he could work with his hands and stay beneath any notice. Over the decades, the welding bay became his routine, but also a space that constantly echoed the old room. The booth was tightly enclosed, his heavy gloves and thick visor narrowing his vision until he was certain he could never predict who might step through the entrance or what might come next. He learned to watch the alley through the narrow gap in his protective gear, his shoulders permanently drawn tight. When a backfire cracked outside or a heavy service door slammed, his breath would catch and his body would brace as if the wire were still on his wrists again. In the shop hours, he moved with the same careful deference. When the foreman raised his voice or questioned a weld, Mateo would immediately agree, nodding and offering extra care. At home, widowed for a decade, he avoided pressing any topic, never letting frustration surface, because he was sure that showing any edge would draw the wrong kind of attention. When the memories of that room rose, he forced his thoughts toward the hum of the transformer or the rhythm of his own breathing, detaching from the images before they could settle, telling himself firmly that they were only old noise. Yet the past did not stay buried. When he tried to explain the ordeal to his daughter, the words fractured in his mouth. He would start with the room, the silence, the cold concrete, but then his voice would stall, the thread snapping, leaving only a tight chest and a heat that rushed up his neck. He realized he felt it again before he even named it—the same weight on his shoulders, the same metallic taste in his mouth, as though the floor beneath him had not changed at all. And when he finally let himself remember the full arc of it, a dark fury would ignite in his stomach, a rage so sharp it made his hands tremble. He blamed himself for not fighting harder, for the silence he had kept when others were hurt, for the choices he thought had sealed his fate. He was certain that danger could appear anywhere, from anyone, and that the only way to endure it was to stay invisible, to keep his thoughts locked away, to never give the past a foothold in the present. Now at seventy, Mateo found his routines fraying. The last two months had brought a new urgency: a pressure gauge on an old compressor had burst with a report that sounded exactly like a rifle shot, and he had frozen in the corner of his garage, unable to move until the echo faded. The shop foreman had noticed his withdrawal, leaving work piling up in the corner because Mateo could no longer bear the sound of metal dropping or the feeling of his boots pinned beneath a fallen crate. He had come to the clinic because his hands no longer trusted him with the torch, because he could not sleep without pacing the hallway, and because he was tired of carrying the weight of a room that had long since been emptied out. He wanted to understand why his body still braced for a door that would not open, what he could do to stop the anger from burning through his chest when the memories returned, and how he might finally forgive himself for surviving it all.
